title: The Wiggling Apples' Secret
markdown:
Whisperwind Orchard smelled of sunshine and secrets. Rafi the apple-picker had rosy cheeks, bright as the ripest fruit, and he hummed a bouncy tune about a squirrel who had found a particularly shiny acorn. Hum-de-dum-dee-doo. Even a grumpy worm might have wiggled its toes. Each plump ruby apple gleamed like a jewel in the afternoon sun and thumped into his sturdy woven basket like a little song of harvest.

Mint the orchard sprite flitted nearby, small enough to ride a ladybug, wings shimmering like freshly fallen dew. Her voice was tiny bells giggling in the breeze. She loved Whisperwind more than anything. She knew every rustling leaf, every busy ant, and she kept a very close eye on Rafi and his precious apples.

Rafi hummed, lost in the cheerful work. Then one apple wiggled. Just a tiny bit at first. Then another gave a little shimmy. And another.

Rafi stopped humming. His happy tune trailed off. “Huh?” He scratched his head and peered into the basket. The apples were not sitting still, being ordinary apples. They were floating. Whoosh. A bright red one drifted lazily up, then another, then a whole bunch, bobbing and weaving like playful bubbles. They formed a line, pointing — a polite apple arrow — toward the oldest, gnarliest tree in the whole orchard. This tree was very, very old. Its branches looked like crinkly arms reaching for the sky. Its bark looked like a wise, wrinkled face full of secrets.

“Mint! Mint, come look. You won’t believe this.” Rafi whispered, even though nobody else was around. A tingle of excitement ran all the way to his toes.

A flash of shimmering light zipped past his nose so fast he blinked. Mint hovered, tiny wings buzzing like a happy hummingbird. “I see it, Rafi. I see it. The Whispering Tree is showing you the way.” She tipped toward the floating fruit. “Kin of my kin,” she said, as if the apples had taught her the words.

The apples continued their march, gliding smoothly, leading Rafi and Mint right up to the base of the ancient tree. The trunk was so wide and massive Rafi could not hug it all the way around. He tried, arms stretching. Grunt. “Nope. Too big.” A little puff of air escaped his cheeks.

Then, on the rough, deeply grooved bark, a tiny door appeared. It had not been there a moment before. It was small enough for Mint to waltz through, and just about big enough for Rafi to squeeze his head in if he tilted it just so. Smooth dark wood, polished by time. A little brass doorknob that gleamed like a tiny golden moon.

“A door?” Rafi whispered, eyes wide as saucers.

“Only for the brave,” Mint squeaked, doing a little loop-de-loop, wings leaving trails of sparkle. “The ancient tree only opens its secrets to those with a courageous heart. You have to knock, Rafi. You have to be brave enough to knock on a door that just appeared.”

Rafi looked at the door. It was so small, so delicate. What if a grumpy badger lived inside, with spectacles and a very stern frown? Or worse, a giant spider wearing a tiny silly hat? His tummy did a little flip-flop, like a fish jumping. Then he remembered the apples, and Mint, and the wonderful secret magic of Whisperwind. He wanted to be brave, like a knight on a quest. He took a deep breath of sweet apple-scented air. “Okay,” he said, a little shaky but firm. He squared his shoulders.

He reached out a hand that felt as big as a giant’s next to the tiny door. He tapped, softly at first, tap-tap-tap. He listened.

Nothing. Not a peep.

“Try again,” Mint urged, hovering close. “Louder. With feeling. Imagine you’re knocking on the door of your best friend.”

Rafi took another breath, puffing out his chest like a proud robin. He knocked TAP-TAP-TAP, putting all his hope and curiosity into it.

Click. The little brass knob turned all by itself. The tiny door swung open with a soft creak, like an old contented sigh.

Inside was not dark or scary. Warm golden light felt like a hug. There was a miniature armchair of soft springy moss, just the size for a very small person. A tiny table held a single perfect glistening berry. The air smelled like the sweetest honey and the warmest sunshine mixed together.

Rafi and Mint did not speak. They looked. Pollen turned in the gold. The moss chair waited. The berry shone. Time stretched, quiet as roots.

On the moss sat a tiny glowing apple, pulsing with a soft warm light, like a tiny beating heart. Not a basket apple. The Heart Apple.

The floating fruit drifted closer to the threshold, as if greeting it. Mint’s bells were almost a whisper. “Kin of my kin.”

Rafi’s heart swelled with a feeling he could not quite name, wonder and quiet accomplishment. He did not need to step inside. Just seeing it, knowing he had found it, was enough.

A magpie, greedy for anything that gleamed, swooped at the open door. Mint zipped. Rafi set his basket down as a shield. The magpie, finding no necklace, only orchard light, flapped off to bother a weather-vane instead. The Heart Apple did not dim.

“You did it, Rafi,” Mint said at last, landing softly on his shoulder, tiny wings fluttering. “You were brave. You followed the apples.”

Rafi grinned, a big apple-cheeked grin. “Kin of my kin,” he said, tasting the phrase like juice. He would not tell anyone else about the door, not really. This was their secret: his, and Mint’s, and the ancient apple tree’s.

The tiny door swung shut with another soft contented sigh. The bark looked ordinary and rough again. The floating apples settled back into the basket, ordinary and ruby, as if they had never danced. A warmth spread through Rafi. He had discovered a bit more magic in the world, and that was even better than the juiciest apple. Tomorrow he would hum an even happier tune, and the Heart Apple would still beat, unseen, among its sisters in the dark.
